stages.a: A colonized block in a closed bag with a filter patch.
stages.v: Antlers form in high in-bag CO2, perhaps 3,000-5,000 ppm with an A-style filter.

stages.a: Knobbly antlers grow up inside the bag; their tips stay pale.
stages.v: Antlers take 3-4 months to reach the bag top and can keep growing for up to a year.

stages.a: The antlers reach the top of the bag.
stages.v: Fruited in the bag, the antlers are "scalped" level with the block once they reach the top.

stages.a: The bag comes off and the antlers meet fresh air.
stages.v: In fresh air, below about 1,000 ppm CO2, the kidney-shaped cap forms. Stripping the bag brings caps back.

stages.a: The antler tips flatten and spread into caps with a pale growing edge.
stages.v: On year-old antlers, caps come back about a month after stripping.

stages.a: Kidney-shaped caps ringed with growth zones, the edge still pale.
stages.v: Fruiting RH 85-95%. Below about 85% the pore surface may not develop properly.

stages.a: Brown spores dust the cap tops.
stages.v: Spore loads are heavy: wear a respirator at harvest.

labels.a: The closed bag keeps CO2 high.
labels.v: Very airtight bags kept one culture stuck as small antlers; very open B patches would probably stunt them.

labels.a: Branching, knobbly stems with no cap.
labels.v: High CO2 in the bag makes antlers instead of a cap.
Lower CO2 (fresh air) makes a cap instead of antlers.

labels.a: A pale band at the edge where the cap is still growing.
Ridges ring the cap as it grows.
The underside is fine pores, not gills.
labels.v: Below about 85% RH the pore surface may not develop properly.

labels.a: Brown spores fall and settle on the caps.
labels.v: Spore loads are heavy; one farm always harvested reishi outdoors.
